h1:
Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
The Complete Visitor Guide
intro: If you only have time for one temple in Chiang Mai, most people point you straight to Wat Phra That Doi Suthep — you get the golden chedi that's the spiritual heart of the city, the long naga staircase you've seen in every photo, and a sweeping view over Chiang Mai from up on the mountain. We've pulled together everything worth knowing before you go: how much the red songthaew costs, what time it opens, the entry fee, whether you can handle the 306 steps, and where the best photos are.
chips: ⛩️ Chedi for those born in the Year of the Goat

blocks.html: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Ratchaworawihan sits on Doi Suthep mountain, about 15 km from central Chiang Mai, roughly a 30–40 minute drive up the hill. The highlight is the golden chedi that enshrines a relic of the Buddha — it's the year-of-birth chedi for people born in the Year of the Goat, and northern Thais consider it a sacred temple everyone should pay respects to at least once. This article draws on the latest information and real reviews from people who've just been.

items: Opening hours: daily 06:00–20:00 (it opens early at 6 a.m., so if you want to beat the heat and the crowds, go early)
Foreigner entry fee: 30 THB (most Thais don't pay an entry fee but can make a merit donation as they wish)
Funicular: about 20 THB extra for the ride up and down, if you'd rather not take the stairs
Time needed: a walk around the grounds takes about 1 hour, not counting travel time

blocks.title: A fee mix-up people make all the time
blocks.html: The 30 THB entry fee and the 20 THB funicular fare are two separate things. If you pay both together at one counter before riding the funicular, it comes to about 50 THB. Some people think the 50 THB is the temple entry fee, when really it already includes the round-trip funicular. If you take the stairs yourself, you only pay the 30 THB.

blocks.text: How to get up Doi Suthep

blocks.html: There's no direct public bus to Doi Suthep. The way most travellers go is by red songthaew (the red shared pickup trucks), followed by renting a motorbike or car, or calling a Grab/taxi. Here's a rough breakdown of the prices so you know what to expect.

items.name: Red songthaew (red shared pickup)
items.blurb: The most popular and cheapest option. The main pickup points are in front of Chiang Mai University (the zoo side) and Chang Phueak Gate on the old-city side. They leave once about 8–10 passengers fill the truck, so you may have to wait a while for it to fill up.
items.meta: One way · pickup at CMU / Chang Phueak Gate

items.name: Charter a red songthaew round trip
items.blurb: If you're a group or don't want to wait for the truck to fill, you can charter a whole songthaew. The driver waits and brings you back — always agree on the price before you get in. Good for groups who want to carry on to Bhubing Palace or the Doi Pui Hmong village afterwards.
items.meta: Whole truck · waits and brings you back

items.name: Rent a motorbike and ride yourself
items.blurb: The most freedom — you ride up via Huay Kaew Road, past Maya and the zoo and on up the hill. But there are lots of curves and it's steep, so if you're not used to mountain roads, be careful, and the road gets slippery in the rain. Motorbike rental in town is just a few hundred baht a day.
items.meta: Via Huay Kaew Road · lots of curves

items.name: Grab / taxi
items.blurb: Comfortable and no waiting, but few cars go up the mountain and the fare is several times the songthaew. Sometimes it's hard to get a driver to accept the trip up, and getting a ride back down from the temple can be tricky. Good if you'll pay for the convenience.
items.meta: Booked via app · hard to get a ride back

items.name: Half-day join-in tour
items.blurb: A van picks you up from your hotel and takes you up Doi Suthep, then adds Bhubing Palace or the Doi Pui Hmong village in the same trip, with a guide along the way. Good if you don't want to plan it yourself — book ahead with an agency in town.
items.meta: Half day · hotel pickup and drop-off

blocks.title: Plan ahead for the trip back down
blocks.html: If you came up by red songthaew on a per-person basis, you'll need to wait for another songthaew at the parking lot up top to fill up for the ride down. Late in the afternoon when there are fewer people, that wait can be long. If you'd rather not risk it, charter a songthaew to wait for you, or arrange a return time with the driver in advance.

From the parking lot up to the temple itself you have to climb, and there are two options. The first is the 306-step naga staircase, with serpent balustrades running down both sides — it's the classic photo spot you've seen on every postcard, and a steady walk up takes about 10–15 minutes. The second is the funicular that pulls you straight up the slope, ideal if you have bad knees, are elderly, or have young kids with you.

items: The stairs — great atmosphere and lovely photos, but the steps are fairly steep, so wear comfortable shoes and bring water
The funicular — fast and easy, about 20 THB extra, good on a scorching day or if you can't manage the climb
Mix and match — plenty of people walk up the stairs for the photos, then take the funicular down to spare their legs

items.name: The golden chedi
items.blurb: The gleaming golden chedi in the centre of the courtyard enshrines a relic of the Buddha. Visitors like to walk three times around it with lit candles for good fortune.

items.name: Chiang Mai city viewpoint
items.blurb: A viewpoint looking out over the city of Chiang Mai stretching out below. On a clear day you can see all the way to the airport, and the mornings are clearer and less crowded.

items.name: Naga staircase and gate arch
items.blurb: Seven-headed serpents stretch down the staircase — an unmistakable photo backdrop. Shoot from the bottom looking up for the best angle.

items.name: Bells around the courtyard
items.blurb: A row of bells you can strike for belief and tradition, ringing out across the temple courtyard. Kids love it, and it's a good corner to capture the atmosphere.

blocks.text: Photo spots and the best time of day

blocks.html: The most-photographed angles are the naga staircase shot from the bottom looking up, the golden chedi against the sky, and the city viewpoint. The best time is early morning, around 06:00–08:00, when the sky is still clear, the sun isn't harsh, and there are few people. From mid-morning to midday is when the tour crowds are thickest.

blocks.title: Dress code and etiquette
blocks.html: The temple has a clear dress code: shoulders and knees must be covered, so shorts and spaghetti-strap tops aren't allowed. You'll need to take your shoes off before entering the buildings, and keep your voice down, since people come here to genuinely pray. If you're not dressed appropriately, there are wraps to borrow at the entrance.

blocks.text: More to see up the mountain

items: Bhubing Palace — about 4 km further up the road, with flower gardens and cool air. It's only open to visitors when there's no royal residence, so check the opening days before you go.
Doi Pui Hmong village — a Hmong village near the summit with souvenirs, coffee, and a viewpoint, good to add on after Bhubing Palace.
Huay Kaew Waterfall / Kruba Srivichai — at the foot of the mountain on the way up, where you can stop for photos at the Kruba Srivichai monument and make a wish before heading up.

faq.q: What time does Wat Phra That Doi Suthep open?
faq.a: It's open daily from 06:00 to 20:00. To avoid the crowds and the heat, go in the early morning, roughly between 6 and 8 a.m. — the sky is clearer and the photos come out better.

faq.q: How much is the entry fee at Wat Phra That Doi Suthep?
faq.a: Foreigners pay a 30 THB entry fee, and the funicular adds about 20 THB more for the ride up and down. If you take the stairs yourself, you only pay the entry fee. Most Thais don't pay an entry fee but can make a merit donation as they wish.

faq.q: How much does the red songthaew up Doi Suthep cost?
faq.a: A red songthaew from in front of Chiang Mai University or Chang Phueak Gate runs about 60 THB per person each way. They leave once about 8–10 passengers fill the truck. If you're carrying on to Bhubing Palace or the Doi Pui Hmong village it gets more expensive with the distance, or you can charter the whole truck.

faq.q: Do I have to climb the 306 steps, or is there another way?
faq.a: No, you don't. There's a funicular up and down for about 20 THB extra, ideal if you have bad knees, are elderly, or have young kids. Plenty of people walk up the stairs for the naga-staircase photos and take the funicular down.

faq.q: What should I wear to enter the temple?
faq.a: Shoulders and knees must be covered — no shorts or spaghetti-strap tops. You'll need to take your shoes off before entering the buildings. If you're not dressed appropriately, there are wraps to borrow at the entrance.
